title: Limit Theorems
summary: Probability is most useful when many random contributions are combined. Two facts then emerge: averages settle down to a constant (the law of large numbers), and the fluctuations around that constant take a universal bell shape (the central limit theorem).…

intro.x: Probability is most useful when many random contributions are combined. Two facts then emerge: averages settle down to a constant (the law of large numbers), and the fluctuations around that constant take a universal bell shape (the central limit theorem). To state them we must first say what it means for a sequence of random variables to converge. This chapter defines the four standard modes of convergence, proves how they relate, proves the Borel–Cantelli lemmas, and then proves the laws of large numbers and the central limit theorem.

blocks.x: Let $X,X_1,X_2,\dots$ be random variables on the same probability space (except for convergence in distribution, where the spaces may differ).
$X_n\to X$ almost surely (a.s.) if $\Prob\bigl(\lim_nX_n=X\bigr)=1$.
$X_n\to X$ in probability, written $X_n\xrightarrow{p}X$, if $\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon)\to0$ for every $\epsilon>0$.
$X_n\to X$ in $L^p$ ($p\ge1$) if $\Exp\abs{X_n-X}^p\to0$.
$X_n\to X$ in distribution, written $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$, if $F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)$ at every $x$ where $F_X$ is continuous.

Let $X_n=1/n$ (deterministic) and $X=0$. Then $F_{X_n}(0)=0$ for all $n$, but $F_X(0)=1$. We would not want to say that $X_n$ fails to converge to $0$, so we ignore the jump point $x=0$. The restriction to continuity points of the limit fixes exactly this.
If $X_n\to X$ a.s., then $X_n\xrightarrow{p}X$.
If $X_n\to X$ in $L^p$, then $X_n\xrightarrow{p}X$.
If $X_n\xrightarrow{p}X$, then $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$.
If $X_n\xrightarrow{d}c$ for a constant $c$, then $X_n\xrightarrow{p}c$.
No other implication holds in general (see the examples below).

(a) Fix $\epsilon>0$ and let $A_n=\{\abs{X_m-X}\le\epsilon\text{ for all }m\ge n\}$. The $A_n$ increase. If $X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)$ then $\omega\in A_n$ for some $n$, so $\Prob(\bigcup_nA_n)\ge\Prob(X_n\to X)=1$. By continuity of probability, $\Prob(A_n)\to1$. Since $\{\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon\}\subseteq A_n^c$, we get $\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon)\to0$.
(b) Markov’s inequality: $\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon)\le\Exp\abs{X_n-X}^p/\epsilon^p\to0$.
(c) Let $x$ be a continuity point of $F=F_X$ and $\epsilon>0$. Then
F_{X_n}(x)=\Prob(X_n\le x)\le\Prob(X\le x+\epsilon)+\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon),

because $X_n\le x$ and $\abs{X_n-X}\le\epsilon$ imply $X\le x+\epsilon$. Similarly $F_{X_n}(x)\ge F(x-\epsilon)-\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon)$. Letting $n\to\infty$: $F(x-\epsilon)\le\liminf F_{X_n}(x)\le\limsup F_{X_n}(x)\le F(x+\epsilon)$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and use continuity of $F$ at $x$.

(d) The CDF of the constant $c$ is $0$ below $c$, $1$ at and above $c$, continuous everywhere except $c$. For $\epsilon>0$ the points $c\pm\epsilon$ are continuity points, so $\Prob(\abs{X_n-c}>\epsilon)\le F_{X_n}(c-\epsilon)+1-F_{X_n}(c+\epsilon)\to0+1-1=0$.

In probability but not almost surely (the “typewriter sequence”). On $\Omega=[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure, let $X_n=\indic_{I_n}$ where $I_n$ runs through the intervals $[0,1]$; $[0,\frac12],[\frac12,1]$; $[0,\frac13],[\frac13,\frac23],[\frac23,1]$; and so on, sweeping across $[0,1]$ with shorter and shorter intervals. Then $\Prob(X_n\ne0)=\abs{I_n}\to0$, so $X_n\xrightarrow{p}0$, yet every $\omega$ is in infinitely many $I_n$, so $X_n(\omega)=1$ infinitely often and $X_n$ converges for no $\omega$.

Almost surely but not in $L^1$. Let $U\sim U(0,1)$ and $X_n=n\indic_{\{U<1/n\}}$. For every $\omega$ with $U(\omega)>0$, $X_n(\omega)=0$ once $n>1/U(\omega)$, so $X_n\to0$ a.s.; but $\Exp[X_n]=n\cdot\frac1n=1\not\to0$. Mass escapes to infinity on a set of vanishing probability.
In distribution but not in probability. Let $X\sim N(0,1)$ and $X_n=-X$. All $X_n$ have the same law as $X$, so $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$, but $\abs{X_n-X}=2\abs X$ does not tend to $0$ in probability.
For events $A_1,A_2,\dots$ define
\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\bigcup_{m=n}^\infty A_m,
the event that infinitely many of the $A_n$ occur (“i.o.” is “infinitely often”). (An outcome is in this set iff for every $n$ it lies in some $A_m$ with $m\ge n$.)
If $\sum_n\Prob(A_n)<\infty$, then $\Prob(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$.

For each $n$, $\{A_k\text{ i.o.}\}\subseteq\bigcup_{m\ge n}A_m$, so by countable subadditivity $\Prob(A_k\text{ i.o.})\le\sum_{m\ge n}\Prob(A_m)$, which is the tail of a convergent series and tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$.
If the events $A_n$ are independent and $\sum_n\Prob(A_n)=\infty$, then $\Prob(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$.

It suffices to show $\Prob\bigl(\bigcap_{m\ge n}A_m^c\bigr)=0$ for every $n$, since then the complement of $\{A_k\text{ i.o.}\}$, which is the union over $n$ of these events, is a countable union of null events. By independence (of the complements, Proposition 3.13) and $1-x\le e^{-x}$, for $N>n$,

\Prob\Bigl(\bigcap_{m=n}^NA_m^c\Bigr)=\prod_{m=n}^N\bigl(1-\Prob(A_m)\bigr)
\le\exp\Bigl(-\sum_{m=n}^N\Prob(A_m)\Bigr)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}0,
because the series diverges. Let $N\to\infty$ using continuity from above.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: independence is essential in the second lemma

blocks.x: Let $U\sim U(0,1)$ and $A_n=\{U<1/n\}$. Then $\sum\Prob(A_n)=\sum1/n=\infty$, but the events are nested, and $\Prob(A_n\text{ i.o.})=\Prob(U=0)=0$. The two lemmas together form a “zero–one law” for independent events: the probability of infinitely many occurrences is $0$ or $1$, according to whether $\sum\Prob(A_n)$ converges or diverges.

A monkey types independently, each key uniformly from $27$ keys. Let $A_k$ be the event that the $k$th block of $5$ consecutive keystrokes spells a fixed word (such as “HELLO”). The $A_k$ are independent with probability $27^{-5}>0$ each, so $\sum\Prob(A_k)=\infty$ and by the second lemma the word appears infinitely often almost surely.
If $\sum_n\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>\epsilon)<\infty$ for every $\epsilon>0$, then $X_n\to X$ almost surely.
If $X_n\xrightarrow{p}X$, then there is a subsequence $X_{n_k}\to X$ almost surely.

(i) For $\epsilon=1/j$, Theorem 11.4 gives $\Prob(\abs{X_n-X}>1/j\text{ i.o.})=0$. The union over $j\in\N$ of these null events is null, and outside it $\abs{X_n-X}\le1/j$ eventually for every $j$, i.e. $X_n\to X$. (ii) Choose $n_1<n_2<\dots$ with $\Prob(\abs{X_{n_k}-X}>2^{-k})<2^{-k}$. By Theorem 11.4, almost surely $\abs{X_{n_k}-X}\le2^{-k}$ for all large $k$.
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and put $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$.
If $\Var(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $S_n/n\xrightarrow{p}\mu$; in fact $\Prob(\abs{S_n/n-\mu}>\epsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\epsilon^2)$.
$\Exp[S_n/n]=\mu$ and $\Var(S_n/n)=n\sigma^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n$ by independence. Apply Chebyshev’s inequality.
The strong law says more: the averages converge for almost every outcome. We prove it under a finite variance using a maximal inequality.
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent with $\Exp[X_i]=0$ and finite variances. Then for every $\lambda>0$,
\Prob\Bigl(\max_{1\le k\le n}\abs{S_k}\ge\lambda\Bigr)\le\frac{\Var(S_n)}{\lambda^2}.
Let $A_k=\{\abs{S_k}\ge\lambda,\ \abs{S_j}<\lambda\ \text{for }j<k\}$, the event that the first exceedance is at time $k$. The $A_k$ are disjoint and their union is the event in question. Then

\Exp[S_n^2]\ge\sum_{k=1}^n\Exp\bigl[S_n^2\indic_{A_k}\bigr]
\ge\sum_{k=1}^n\Exp\bigl[\bigl(S_k^2+2S_k(S_n-S_k)\bigr)\indic_{A_k}\bigr],

using $S_n^2=S_k^2+2S_k(S_n-S_k)+(S_n-S_k)^2\ge S_k^2+2S_k(S_n-S_k)$. Now $S_k\indic_{A_k}$ is a function of $X_1,\dots,X_k$ and $S_n-S_k$ of $X_{k+1},\dots,X_n$, so they are independent and $\Exp[S_k(S_n-S_k)\indic_{A_k}]=\Exp[S_k\indic_{A_k}]\Exp[S_n-S_k]=0$. Hence $\Exp[S_n^2]\ge\sum_k\Exp[S_k^2\indic_{A_k}]\ge\lambda^2\sum_k\Prob(A_k)$, because $S_k^2\ge\lambda^2$ on $A_k$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Strong law of large numbers, finite-variance version

blocks.x: If $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2<\infty$, then $S_n/n\to\mu$ almost surely.
Replacing $X_i$ by $X_i-\mu$ we may assume $\mu=0$.

Step 1: along squares. By Chebyshev, $\Prob(\abs{S_{k^2}}>\epsilon k^2)\le k^2\sigma^2/(\epsilon^2k^4)=\sigma^2/(\epsilon^2k^2)$, which is summable in $k$. By Theorem 11.7(i) (applied to the sequence $S_{k^2}/k^2$), $S_{k^2}/k^2\to0$ almost surely.

Step 2: between squares. Let $D_k=\max_{k^2\le n<(k+1)^2}\abs{S_n-S_{k^2}}$. The variables $S_n-S_{k^2}$ are partial sums of $X_{k^2+1},\dots$, a block of $(k+1)^2-1-k^2=2k$ independent terms. By Kolmogorov’s inequality,
\Prob(D_k\ge\epsilon k^2)\le\frac{2k\sigma^2}{\epsilon^2k^4}=\frac{2\sigma^2}{\epsilon^2k^3},
which is summable. By Theorem 11.7(i), $D_k/k^2\to0$ almost surely.
Step 3. For $k^2\le n<(k+1)^2$ we have $n\ge k^2$ and $\abs{S_n}\le\abs{S_{k^2}}+D_k$, so $\abs{S_n/n}\le\abs{S_{k^2}}/k^2+D_k/k^2\to0$ almost surely.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the strong law needs only a finite mean

blocks.x: Kolmogorov’s strong law: if $X_i$ are i.i.d. and $\Exp\abs{X_1}<\infty$, then $S_n/n\to\Exp[X_1]$ almost surely; conversely if $\Exp\abs{X_1}=\infty$ then $\limsup\abs{S_n}/n=\infty$ almost surely. The proof for a mere first moment uses truncation and is due to Etemadi (see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 2.4); we use the result without proving it. The Cauchy distribution (Example 9.16) shows that without a mean there is no law of large numbers at all.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: the law of large numbers does not say that losses are “due” to be balanced

blocks.x: The law says $S_n/n\to\mu$, not that $S_n-n\mu$ returns to zero. After a streak of $10$ heads, the next toss is still $50\%$ heads. The excess heads are not cancelled by later tails; they are diluted by the growing denominator. The “gambler’s fallacy” confuses these two statements.
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with a continuous CDF $F$, and let $F_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\indic_{\{X_i\le x\}}$ be the empirical CDF. Then $\sup_x\abs{F_n(x)-F(x)}\to0$ almost surely.

Fix $m\ge1$ and pick points $-\infty=x_0<x_1<\dots<x_m=\infty$ with $F(x_j)=j/m$ (possible since $F$ is continuous). For each $j$, $F_n(x_j)\to F(x_j)$ almost surely by the strong law applied to the indicators. So almost surely $F_n(x_j)\to F(x_j)$ for all $j=0,\dots,m$ simultaneously (finite intersection). For $x\in[x_{j-1},x_j]$, by monotonicity of $F_n$ and $F$,
F_n(x)-F(x)\le F_n(x_j)-F(x_{j-1})=F_n(x_j)-F(x_j)+\tfrac1m,
and similarly $F_n(x)-F(x)\ge F_n(x_{j-1})-F(x_{j-1})-\tfrac1m$. Hence $\limsup_n\sup_x\abs{F_n(x)-F(x)}\le\tfrac1m$ almost surely. Let $m\to\infty$ along the integers.
The law of large numbers says $S_n/n-\mu\to0$. To see the fluctuations we rescale by $\sqrt n$.
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. Then
\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).
We need two lemmas.
For real $x$, define $R(x)=e^{ix}-1-ix+\tfrac12x^2$. Then $\abs{R(x)}\le\min\bigl(\abs x^3/6,\ x^2\bigr)$.

Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives $e^{ix}=1+ix+i^2\int_0^x(x-s)e^{is}ds$ and $e^{ix}=1+ix-\tfrac12x^2+\frac{i^3}2\int_0^x(x-s)^2e^{is}ds$. Since $\abs{e^{is}}=1$, the first gives $\abs{e^{ix}-1-ix}\le x^2/2$ and the second gives $\abs{R(x)}\le\abs x^3/6$. Also $\abs{R(x)}\le\abs{e^{ix}-1-ix}+x^2/2\le x^2$.
If complex numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n,b_1,\dots,b_n$ have modulus at most $1$, then $\bigl\lvert\prod a_i-\prod b_i\bigr\rvert\le\sum\abs{a_i-b_i}$.
Telescope: $\prod_{i=1}^na_i-\prod_{i=1}^nb_i=\sum_{k=1}^n \bigl(\prod_{i<k}b_i\bigr)(a_k-b_k)\bigl(\prod_{i>k}a_i\bigr)$, and each product of unimodular-bounded factors has modulus at most $1$.
Replace $X_i$ by $(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$, so assume $\mu=0$, $\sigma=1$. Let $\varphi$ be the characteristic function of $X_1$. Since the $X_i$ are independent,
\varphi_{S_n/\sqrt n}(t)=\varphi\bigl(t/\sqrt n\bigr)^n .
We must show this tends to $e^{-t^2/2}$ for each fixed $t$. Put $u=t/\sqrt n$. By Lemma 11.13 and $\Exp[X]=0$, $\Exp[X^2]=1$,
\varphi(u)=\Exp[e^{iuX}]=1-\tfrac12u^2+\Exp[R(uX)]=1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+\Exp[R(uX)].
Let $b=e^{-t^2/(2n)}$; then $b^n=e^{-t^2/2}$ exactly. Both $\abs{\varphi(u)}\le1$ and $b\le1$, so by Lemma 11.14

\bigl\lvert\varphi(u)^n-b^n\bigr\rvert\le n\abs{\varphi(u)-b}
\le n\Bigl\lvert1-\frac{t^2}{2n}-e^{-t^2/(2n)}\Bigr\rvert+n\,\Exp\abs{R(uX)}.
For the first term use $\abs{1-z-e^{-z}}\le z^2/2$ for $z\ge0$ with $z=t^2/(2n)$: it is at most $n\cdot t^4/(8n^2)\to0$. For the second,
n\,\Exp\abs{R(uX)}\le\Exp\Bigl[\min\Bigl(\frac{\abs t^3\abs X^3}{6\sqrt n},\ t^2X^2\Bigr)\Bigr].

For each outcome the quantity inside tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$, and it is dominated by $t^2X^2$, which is integrable. By dominated convergence the expectation tends to $0$. Hence $\varphi_{S_n/\sqrt n}(t)\to e^{-t^2/2}$, the characteristic function of $N(0,1)$ (Example 9.15). By L'evy’s continuity theorem (Theorem 9.14(vi), proved in Chapter 15), $S_n/\sqrt n\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$.
If $X_n\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, then $(X_n-np)/\sqrt{npq}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$.
$X_n$ is a sum of $n$ i.i.d. Bernoulli$(p)$ variables (mean $p$, variance $pq$).

For $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(100,\tfrac12)$, $\mu=50$, $\sigma=5$. The event $\{X\ge60\}$ equals $\{X>59.5\}$ in the integer-valued sense, so $\Prob(X\ge60)\approx1-\Phi\bigl(\tfrac{59.5-50}5\bigr)=1-\Phi(1.9)\approx0.0287$, compared with the exact value $0.0284$. Without the $\tfrac12$ correction the answer would be $1-\Phi(2)=0.0228$, noticeably worse.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: what the CLT does and does not say

blocks.x: The CLT is about the centre of the distribution at scale $\sqrt n$. It gives no information about tail probabilities at a fixed multiple of $n$ (use Chernoff or Hoeffding), nor, for a fixed $n$, about the error. The Berry–Esseen theorem (cited, not proved) bounds the error: $\sup_x\abs{F_n(x)-\Phi(x)}\le C\,\Exp\abs{X_1-\mu}^3/(\sigma^3\sqrt n)$ with an absolute constant $C<0.5$. The rate $n^{-1/2}$ cannot be improved in general.

Finite variance is essential. For distributions with infinite variance the normalised sums, if they converge at all, converge to stable laws (the Cauchy law is the stable law of index $1$), and the right scaling is not $\sqrt n$.

Convergence is in distribution: the sequence $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ does not converge almost surely, or in probability; it keeps fluctuating at order $1$ forever (this is made precise by the law of the iterated logarithm, cited).
The CLT extends to non-identically distributed summands under the Lindeberg condition, and to random vectors (the multivariate CLT, with limit $N(0,\Sigma)$); we state these without proof.

sections.title: Slutsky’s theorem and the delta method

blocks.x: Suppose $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$ and $Y_n\xrightarrow{p}c$ for a constant $c$. Then $X_n+Y_n\xrightarrow{d}X+c$ and $X_nY_n\xrightarrow{d}cX$.

Sum. Let $x$ be a continuity point of $F_{X+c}$, i.e. $x-c$ is a continuity point of $F_X$. For $\epsilon>0$ chosen so that $x-c\pm\epsilon$ are continuity points of $F_X$ (all but countably many $\epsilon$ qualify),

\Prob(X_n\le x-c-\epsilon)-\Prob(\abs{Y_n-c}>\epsilon)\le\Prob(X_n+Y_n\le x)
\le\Prob(X_n\le x-c+\epsilon)+\Prob(\abs{Y_n-c}>\epsilon).
Let $n\to\infty$: $F_X(x-c-\epsilon)\le\liminf\le\limsup\le F_X(x-c+\epsilon)$; now let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ through admissible values, using continuity of $F_X$ at $x-c$.

Product. Write $X_nY_n=cX_n+X_n(Y_n-c)$. First $cX_n\xrightarrow{d}cX$ (if $c\ne0$ the CDFs transform by rescaling the argument; if $c=0$ the limit is the point mass at $0$ and this is trivial). Second, $X_n(Y_n-c)\xrightarrow{p}0$: given $\delta,\eta>0$ choose $K$ so that $\Prob(\abs X\ge K)<\eta$ with $\pm K$ continuity points of $F_X$; then $\Prob(\abs{X_n(Y_n-c)}>\delta)\le\Prob(\abs{X_n}>K)+\Prob(\abs{Y_n-c}>\delta/K)$, whose $\limsup$ is at most $\eta$. Conclude by the sum case applied to $cX_n$ and $X_n(Y_n-c)$.
Suppose $\sqrt n(T_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\tau^2)$ and $g$ is differentiable at $\theta$. Then $\sqrt n\bigl(g(T_n)-g(\theta)\bigr)\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(0,\,g'(\theta)^2\tau^2\bigr)$.

First $T_n\xrightarrow{p}\theta$, since $T_n-\theta=\frac1{\sqrt n}\cdot\sqrt n(T_n-\theta)$ is a product of a sequence tending to $0$ and a convergent-in-distribution sequence (Slutsky). By differentiability, $g(t)-g(\theta)=g'(\theta)(t-\theta)+r(t)(t-\theta)$ where $r(t)\to0$ as $t\to\theta$ ($r(\theta)=0$). Hence
\sqrt n\bigl(g(T_n)-g(\theta)\bigr)=g'(\theta)\sqrt n(T_n-\theta)+r(T_n)\sqrt n(T_n-\theta).

Since $T_n\xrightarrow{p}\theta$ and $r$ is continuous at $\theta$, $r(T_n)\xrightarrow{p}0$ (for any $\epsilon$ pick $\delta$ with $\abs{r(t)}<\epsilon$ for $\abs{t-\theta}<\delta$). By Slutsky the last term tends to $0$ in probability and the first term tends in distribution to $N(0,g'(\theta)^2\tau^2)$; apply Slutsky’s sum rule.

Let $\bar X_n$ be the average of $n$ i.i.d. Poisson$(\lambda)$ variables. By the CLT, $\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\lambda)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\lambda)$. With $g(x)=\sqrt x$, $g'(\lambda)=1/(2\sqrt\lambda)$, so $\sqrt n(\sqrt{\bar X_n}-\sqrt\lambda)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\tfrac14)$. The limiting variance does not depend on $\lambda$: the square root stabilises the variance, which is why $\sqrt{\text{count}}$ is used in practice.

Averages converge: LLN (weak if convergence in probability suffices, strong for almost sure). Distribution of the average at scale $1/\sqrt n$: CLT. Probability of a large deviation at scale $n$: Chernoff/Hoeffding/Cram'er. Smooth function of an average: delta method. Infinite variance or infinite mean: the classical theorems do not apply; check for stable laws.
Prove that if $X_n\xrightarrow{p}X$ and $g$ is continuous then $g(X_n)\xrightarrow{p}g(X)$ (first for uniformly continuous $g$, or for bounded $X$).
Let $X_n\sim\mathrm{Exp}(n)$. Show $X_n\to0$ in probability, almost surely (use Borel–Cantelli with independent copies), and in $L^1$.

Show that if $\sum_n\Prob(\abs{X_n}>\epsilon)<\infty$ for all $\epsilon$ then $X_n\to0$ a.s.; give an example where $X_n\to0$ in probability but $\sum\Prob(\abs{X_n}>\epsilon)=\infty$ for some $\epsilon$.
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. $U(0,1)$ and $M_n=\max_{i\le n}X_i$. Show $M_n\to1$ almost surely, and that $n(1-M_n)\xrightarrow{d}\mathrm{Exp}(1)$.
Use the CLT to approximate the probability that the sum of $100$ fair dice exceeds $370$.
Show the CLT implies that $\Prob(S_n>n\mu)\to\tfrac12$. Does the almost sure version hold (does $S_n-n\mu$ change sign infinitely often)?

Prove that if $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$ and $g$ is continuous then $g(X_n)\xrightarrow{d}g(X)$ (continuous mapping theorem) for bounded continuous $g$, using the characterisation $\Exp[g(X_n)]\to\Exp[g(X)]$ (cited).
Let $X_n$ be the number of fixed points of a random permutation of $n$ elements. Show using inclusion–exclusion that $\Prob(X_n=k)\to e^{-1}/k!$ (Poisson$(1)$ limit).

(Challenge) Prove the weak law of large numbers for i.i.d. variables with $\Exp\abs{X_1}<\infty$ only (truncate at level $\epsilon n$, use Chebyshev on the truncated part and dominated convergence on the remainder).
